claims.text: A high-entropy alloy is constrained here to be a solid solution containing at least five elements, each at no less than 5 atomic percent.
The starting material is a Nb-Ta-rich, roughly equiatomic alloy with at least five elements and a simple BCC structure.
Increasing titanium at the expense of niobium and tantalum enhances superconductivity in a qualifying single-phase HEA.
Titanium enrichment increases electron-phonon coupling strength.
Titanium enrichment beneficially modifies or optimizes the electronic density of states near the Fermi level.
The proposed titanium-induced electronic changes counteract disorder-induced scattering in HEAs.
Stronger pairing interactions caused by titanium produce a higher superconducting critical temperature.
Stronger pairing interactions caused by titanium produce a higher upper critical field.
A homogeneous single BCC phase with minimal secondary precipitation allows superconductivity changes to be attributed to electronic structure rather than microstructural artifacts.
Identical high-energy-milling and pressureless-sintering conditions ensure comparable microstructures and phase purity across the alloy series.
Both Tc and Hc2 will be higher in titanium-enriched alloys than in the Nb-Ta-rich baseline.
Tc and Hc2 will increase progressively as titanium content increases while the alloy remains single-phase BCC.
Type-A BCC HEA superconductors have reported Tc values of approximately 4-9 K.
A Nb-Ta-dominated baseline can be assigned an upper critical field around 12 T.
The hypothesis applies only while a single-phase solid solution is preserved and significant intermetallic precipitation is absent.
Secondary phases or excessive lattice distortion could independently alter superconducting behavior.
Disorder and lattice strain may compete with the proposed titanium-induced enhancement.
Local chemical inhomogeneity and phase instability near compositional boundaries may influence superconducting properties.

contradictions.description: The intervention and boundary require the titanium-enriched specimens to remain single-phase BCC, but the falsification rule treats formation of secondary phases as falsification. Secondary-phase formation instead violates the stated applicability conditions and confounds the intended mechanistic test.
